title: Part 1
text: Ice grows over a giant continent, and the shallow sea around a small armored fish drains away.

title: Part 2
text: That was the world at the end of the Ordovician Period, about 444 million years ago.
nxt: Sacabambaspis, a jawless fish about twenty-five centimeters long, lived shortly before it, roughly 450 million years ago.

title: Part 3
text: Glaciers grew over the huge southern landmass called Gondwana. Sea levels dropped, and the shallow seas where many animals lived shrank away.
nxt: Then, as the ice later melted, parts of the ocean ran low on oxygen. Together, these changes helped cause one of the biggest mass extinctions in Earth's history.

title: Part 4
text: Did any jawless fish make it to the present day? Yes, but not armored ones. Lampreys and hagfish are the only living jawless fish.
nxt: They have slimy, soft, eel-like bodies, and no bony armor. Some scientists think their ancestors lost armor along the way, while others think they never had it.

title: Part 5
text: Meanwhile, another group had found a new trick. Scientists think that parts of the gill supports, the bones that hold up the gills, were reshaped into hinged jaws.
nxt: That change gave rise to the jawed vertebrates, which include sharks, bony fish, and us.

title: Part 6
text: By the Devonian Period, more than sixty million years after Sacabambaspis, armored jawed fish called placoderms ruled the seas.
nxt: The most famous, Dunkleosteus, had bony plates in its mouth that worked like blades. For years, people said it grew to nine meters or more.

title: Part 7
text: Sacabambaspis was not our great-grandparent. It was a member of a side branch of the family tree of vertebrates.
nxt: But the traits that animals like it show us, including bone and a head with sense organs, were built piece by piece over tens of millions of years.
